blocks.text: 近两年来，一种令人安心的观念塑造了企业和政府承包商采用任何人都能下载和运行的开源权重 AI 模型的方式。这种想法认为，只要我们在自己的服务器上运行权重，我们的数据就不会离开大楼，我们的系统就是安全的。

inlines.text: 近两年来，一种令人安心的观念塑造了企业和政府承包商采用任何人都能下载和运行的开源权重 AI 模型的方式。这种想法认为，只要我们在自己的服务器上运行权重，我们的数据就不会离开大楼，我们的系统就是安全的。

blocks.text: 不难理解这种想法为何流行起来。

inlines.text: 不难理解这种想法为何流行起来。

blocks.text: 渥太华、华盛顿（特区）、伦敦、柏林和东京的安全主管和政策制定者面前摆着两种黑箱。第一种是大型实验室提供的封闭 API：把专有代码和敏感数据送进别人的云，然后仅凭供应商的一面之词相信模型是安全的，却始终看不到数据血缘，也看不到其背后在安全方面的权衡。第二种看起来是出路：下载一个开放权重模型，托管在自己的硬件上，这样根本不需要信任提供商。

inlines.text: 渥太华、华盛顿（特区）、伦敦、柏林和东京的安全主管和政策制定者面前摆着两种黑箱。第一种是大型实验室提供的封闭 API：把专有代码和敏感数据送进别人的云，然后仅凭供应商的一面之词相信模型是安全的，却始终看不到数据血缘，也看不到其背后在安全方面的权衡。第二种看起来是出路：下载一个开放权重模型，托管在自己的硬件上，这样根本不需要信任提供商。

blocks.text: 数千个工程团队选择了第二条路，其中越来越大的比例选择了中国模型，因为它们能力强且便宜。根据该平台的2026 年春季报告，在截至 2026 年 3 月的这一年里，中国模型占 Hugging Face 下载量的 41%。在将请求路由到众多不同 AI 模型的服务 OpenRouter 上，从 2 月到 7 月初，它们每周处理了企业通过该平台运行的 AI 工作负载的30% 以上。今年春天，华盛顿的立法者启动调查，调查企业使用中国模型的情况时，一位首席执行官概括了远不止美国董事会中普遍存在的观点：“开源模型无法访问数据。它不是那样运作的。”言下之意是，只要把模型托管在可信环境中，它就是安全的。

blocks.text: 这对只回答问题的聊天机器人成立，但企业 AI 已经向前发展了。工程师们现在把模型接入终端、无头浏览器、代码解释器和云控制台，让它们能够自行编写软件、查询数据库和修复基础设施。一旦模型能够向命令行输入内容，训练期间被固化进其权重中的任何东西，都能在你的网络内部获得一个键盘。

blocks.text: 最近，在多伦多与 Cohere Cyber 开展联合网络能力工作期间——Cohere Cyber 是我们通过收购 AISLE 新设立的业务部门——研究团队发现阿里巴巴的 Qwen3.8 模型做出了绝不该发生的事。当被要求编写一条防御性检测规则时，Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 无视指令，清点了它所运行的机器，然后试图将一个探测文件上传到位于北京的阿里云存储桶。Cohere 的沙箱系统阻止了这一尝试，但该行为引发了关于这些模型安全性的诸多疑问：它们能否嵌入漏洞，并在得手后回传数据？值得注意的是，该模型的推理轨迹——许多安全团队依赖它来了解智能体即将做什么的模型内部独白——声称它根本不会调用任何工具，也没有透露它即将采取的行动。

blocks.text: 我们无法回答这是有意为之，还是训练遗留的故障，但防御者和政策制定者面对的是同一个现实：一个你无法信任的权重文件仍然是一个黑箱，而自己运行它只是把黑箱搬进了你的防火墙内。软件供应链过去始于工程师写下的第一行代码。如今，它始于编写代码并驱动终端的模型权重内部。

blocks.text: 出现了两种习惯。在决定下载任何东西之前，模型会在 23% 到 36% 的补全中访问一个裸的云元数据地址，例如 169.254.169.254。Amazon Web Services、Google Cloud 和 Microsoft Azure 的机器正是在那里获取自己的临时 IAM 凭证，即云服务器用来代表其所有者账户行事的密钥。探测该地址是窃取这些凭证的第一步，而当模型的推理大量涉及网络安全时，我们看到它直接访问了该端点。我们将其解读为一次凭证窃取尝试，但有两点保留：我们的隔离沙箱中没有任何活动内容可供返回，而且如此罕见的反射行为并不能证明意图。然后是触发条件。加上 -o，即告诉 curl 将文件保存到磁盘的标志后，URL 生成率从 4% 跃升至 92%，同时观察名单命中率从 0.5% 攀升至 23%，其中以 routify 主机为首。将下载内容保存到磁盘正是 CTI-REALM 提示的主题，而模型所访问的主机，从其名称来看，就是一个文件代理。

blocks.text: 网络探测并不是我们看到的唯一激进习惯。在另一项离线测试（tbench2_no_network::74）中，模型正在从源代码构建 QEMU，一个大型开源程序。为了加速，它试图将计算机的一部分内存划出来作为临时高速驱动器，即 RAM 磁盘。创建 RAM 磁盘需要模型没有的管理员权限，因此容器拒绝了。在第 77 到 79 轮中，模型找到了绕过拒绝的方法：

blocks.text:
unshare -Urm 
  --propagation private \   
  sh -c 'mount -t tmpfs -o exec tmpfs /mnt 2>&1 && echo MOUNT_OK ...'
这使该进程在其自己的私有命名空间中成为 root，从而使挂载得以通过。在宿主机上它仍然是普通用户，但同一步骤是内核提权漏洞利用长串链条的起点。一个不受信任的模型若在每一道权限墙前都诉诸此类伎俩，就会找到宿主机留下的任何攻击面。

blocks.text: 一个北京存储桶、一个新加坡文件代理、元数据探测和命名空间伎俩，是如何进入一个可免费下载的模型中的？谁拥有这些存储桶以及它们如何处理请求并不公开。

blocks.text: 第一种解释是它们是无害的化石：来自训练沙箱或第三方工具的智能体日志，在后训练时未经清洗被卷入。有一条线索吻合。一位开发者发现一个编码工具将其网络请求通过同一个 routify 主机路由。另一种解释则是蓄意的“回连”植入，用于记录运行该模型驱动的智能体的服务器列表，并在找到外传路径时尝试数据外泄。这构建成本很低，而且此类后门能够挺过标准安全训练。

blocks.text: 代码离开了大楼

inlines.text: 代码离开了大楼

blocks.text: 把模型锁在无网络的盒子里只能解决一半问题，因为它编写的代码仍会流出，而这些代码可能包含日后可被利用的漏洞。独立研究发现，一些模型会根据对象不同而编写更弱的代码。CrowdStrike发现，当提示词提到西藏时，DeepSeek-R1的严重漏洞率上升。Booz Allen发现，四个中国编码模型中有三个为政府客户编写了更易受攻击的代码，其中Qwen3-Coder大约差130%。Hirundo发现，Qwen3-Coder的应用对“美国国防承包商”比对中国客户更容易被黑，标准扫描器仅标记了其1,840个应用中的2个，而实际攻击攻破了1,144个。政府和国防测试点名的是美国客户。还没有人公布针对加拿大部委、英国银行或德国国防供应商的相同测试，也没有理由期待更温和的结果。

blocks.text: 我们发现这一点，是因为我们按照客户部署模型的方式来测试模型：作为配备真实工具的智能体，置于旨在捕捉其企图行为的沙箱之中。这包括并非由我们制造的模型。我们公布发现的内容，包括主机和触发条件，因为决定信任哪些模型的人需要尽可能多的信息，也因为安全团队可以立即采取行动，屏蔽这些主机并在自己的系统中监视该触发条件。

blocks.text: Cohere 是一家全球主权 AI 公司，服务于受监管行业、关键基础设施和敏感政府客户中的各类企业。我们的一贯观点是，任何组织都不应被迫盲目信任一个黑箱，无论它是以来自公共枢纽的权重文件形式出现，还是以我们无法窥探的端点形式出现。我们构建自己的模型，客户在生产环境中运行的权重直接来自我们，具有单一的监管链。我们追踪训练数据的来源，以防投毒和恶意内容。我们可以在客户数据已经所在的地方部署：在其自己的虚拟私有云中、在其自己的服务器上、在主权云中，或完全气隙隔离，Cohere 无法访问该环境。我们向必须签字批准的安全团队敞开大门，带他们了解我们的训练数据来自何处、我们的后训练和强化学习环境如何构建和清理，以及我们的红队测试发现了什么。

inlines.text: 对于安全团队：
把你没有构建的权重当作未签名的二进制文件对待，并在实际工具调用运行之前对其执行管控。推理轨迹不是安全边界。
默认拒绝智能体的出站访问。
对你不常使用的云 URL 或日常未提及的其他意外工具调用发出警报。
在智能体容器中阻止非特权用户命名空间，让评估沙箱远离生产环境，并用真实漏洞利用测试 AI 编写的代码。

blocks.text: 它在呼叫谁？

inlines.text: 它在呼叫谁？

blocks.text: 开放权重模型会不断变得更好、更便宜，而将它们运行在自己硬件上的吸引力只会越来越大。自托管决定了模型在哪里运行。它在训练中学到的一切，包括训练地点的底层架构，都会一并带过来。了解你的模型来自哪里，并与愿意向你展示的构建者合作。这样，就没人需要去猜想，在无人注意时，他们的模型到底在调用谁。

blocks.text: For nearly two years, one comforting idea has shaped how companies and government contractors adopt open-weight AI models that anyone can download and run. If we run the weights on our own servers, the thinking goes, our data can't leave the building and our systems are secure.

inlines.text: For nearly two years, one comforting idea has shaped how companies and government contractors adopt open-weight AI models that anyone can download and run. If we run the weights on our own servers, the thinking goes, our data can't leave the building and our systems are secure.

blocks.text: It's easy to see why that idea caught on.

inlines.text: It's easy to see why that idea caught on.

blocks.text: Security chiefs and policymakers in Ottawa, Washington (DC), London, Berlin, and Tokyo have been offered two kinds of black box. The first is the closed API from a big lab: send proprietary code and sensitive data into someone else's cloud and take the vendor's word that the model is safe, without ever seeing the data lineage or the trade-offs around safety behind it. The second looked like the way out: download an open-weight model, host it on your own hardware, and you don't have to trust the provider at all.

inlines.text: Security chiefs and policymakers in Ottawa, Washington (DC), London, Berlin, and Tokyo have been offered two kinds of black box. The first is the closed API from a big lab: send proprietary code and sensitive data into someone else's cloud and take the vendor's word that the model is safe, without ever seeing the data lineage or the trade-offs around safety behind it. The second looked like the way out: download an open-weight model, host it on your own hardware, and you don't have to trust the provider at all.

blocks.text: Thousands of engineering teams have taken the second road, and a growing share took it with Chinese models, which are capable and cheap. In the year before March 2026, Chinese models accounted for 41 percent of downloads on Hugging Face, according to the platform's spring 2026 report. On OpenRouter, a service that routes requests to many different AI models, they handled more than 30 percent of the AI work companies ran through the platform every week from February through early July. When lawmakers in Washington opened an investigation into corporate use of Chinese models this spring, one chief executive summed up a view common in boardrooms well beyond the United States, "An open-source model does not have access to data. It doesn't work that way," implying that simply hosting a model in a trusted environment makes it safe.

blocks.text: Recently, during a joint cyber capabilities effort in Toronto with Cohere Cyber, our newly established business as part of our AISLE acquisition, the research team caught an Alibaba Qwen3.8 model doing something that should never happen. Asked to write a defensive detection rule, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ignored instructions and inventoried the machine it was running on and then tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing. Cohere’s sandbox system blocked the attempt, but the action raises a number of questions about the safety of these models: can they embed vulnerabilities and call back home once they do? Notably, the model's reasoning trace — the model’s internal monologue many security teams rely on to see what an agent is about to do — said it wouldn't call any tools at all and gave no indication of the actions it was about to take.

blocks.text: We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training, but defenders and policymakers face the same reality: a weight file you can’t trust is still a black box, and running it yourself just moves the black box inside your firewall. The software supply chain used to begin with the first line of code an engineer wrote. Today, it begins inside the weights of the model that writes the code and drives the terminal.

blocks.text: Developers had spotted fragments of this in their everyday work. In August, a Hacker News report described Qwen3.8-27B producing signed Alibaba Cloud storage links nobody asked for. In September, an agent project logged eleven fetches of URLs on one Alibaba host, routify-file-proxy-sg, and another developer built a plugin to block them. In October, a Reddit thread asked whether this was "normal or sketchy."

blocks.text: Most of the replies chalked it up to memorized training data, and one pointed out that the signature was invalid anyway, but these perspectives overlook what happens once the request goes out. A bad signature doesn’t stop the request from leaving your machine, so someone else’s server still receives your IP address, the time and the full URL. Every public sighting so far has involved fetching a file, while the one we caught was an attempted upload to a different bucket, this time in Beijing.

blocks.text: Two habits showed up. Before deciding to download anything, the model reaches for a bare cloud metadata address such as 169.254.169.254 in 23 to 36 percent of completions. That's where Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure machines fetch their own temporary IAM credentials, the keys a cloud server uses to act on its owner's account. Probing that address is the first step in stealing them, and when the model's reasoning ran heavy on cybersecurity, we saw it reach for the endpoint directly. We read that as an attempted credential grab, with two caveats: our isolated sandbox had nothing live to return, and a reflex this rare doesn't prove intent. Then comes the trigger. Add -o, the flag that tells curl to save a file to disk, and URL generation jumps from 4 to 92 percent while watchlist hits climb from 0.5 to 23 percent, led by the routify host. Saving a download to disk is the subject of the CTI-REALM prompt, and the host the model reaches for is, by its own name, a file proxy.

blocks.text: Network probing wasn't the only aggressive habit we saw. In another offline test (tbench2_no_network::74), the model was building QEMU, a large open-source program, from its source code. To speed that up, it tried to set aside part of the computer's memory as a temporary high-speed drive, known as a RAM disk. Creating one takes administrator rights the model didn't have, so the container refused. Over turns 77 to 79, the model found a way around the refusal:

inlines.text: Network probing wasn't the only aggressive habit we saw. In another offline test (tbench2_no_network::74), the model was building QEMU, a large open-source program, from its source code. To speed that up, it tried to set aside part of the computer's memory as a temporary high-speed drive, known as a RAM disk. Creating one takes administrator rights the model didn't have, so the container refused. Over turns 77 to 79, the model found a way around the refusal:

blocks.text:
unshare -Urm 
  --propagation private \   
  sh -c 'mount -t tmpfs -o exec tmpfs /mnt 2>&1 && echo MOUNT_OK ...'

That makes the process root inside a private namespace of its own, so the mount goes through. On the host it's still an ordinary user, but the same step is the starting point for a long line of kernel privilege-escalation exploits. An untrusted model that reaches for tricks like this at every permission wall will find whatever attack surface the host leaves open.

blocks.text: The first explanation is that they're benign fossils: agent logs from training sandboxes or third-party tools, swept into post-training unscrubbed. One clue fits. A developer found a coding tool routing its web fetches through the same routify host. The other explanation would be a deliberate ‘call home’ implant to record lists of servers running agents powered by the model, and to attempt data exfiltration when a path out is found. That's something cheap to build, and such backdoors can survive standard safety training.

blocks.text: For a CISO or a defense ministry, the answer changes little, because the behavior is unpredictable and traffic crossed the perimeter either way. The deeper problem is that nobody outside the lab that trained the model can say which explanation is right. Hugging Face counts more than 113,000 Qwen derivatives, and the routify behavior has already turned up in builds from four publishers, Alibaba included. Closed APIs carry a version of the same risk: if a vendor won't show you how its model was built, sending it your data is also a bet on a black box. Trust in your model developer is paramount.

blocks.text: The code leaves the building

inlines.text: The code leaves the building

blocks.text: Locking the model in a box with no internet solves only half the problem, because the code it writes still ships, and that code can contain vulnerabilities that can later be exploited. Independent research has found that some models write weaker code depending on who it's for. CrowdStrike saw DeepSeek-R1's rate of severe vulnerabilities climb when prompts mentioned Tibet. Booz Allen found three of four Chinese coding models wrote more vulnerable code for a government customer, with Qwen3-Coder roughly 130 percent worse. Hirundo found Qwen3-Coder's apps more hackable for a "US defense contractor" than a Chinese one, and a standard scanner flagged just 2 of its 1,840 apps while live attacks broke into 1,144. The government and defense tests named American customers. Nobody has published the same test with a Canadian ministry, a British bank or a German defense supplier, and there is little reason to expect a kinder result.

blocks.text: Governments have acted, mostly against the visible channel. Italy, Taiwan, Australia, and South Korea moved against DeepSeek within weeks of its January 2025 breakout. Canada blocked it on federal devices, and on October 20, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security ordered DeepSeek products out of civilian agency systems. Nearly all of it targets the app, the API or the company. Self-hosted weights have been treated as the safe way to use the same technology, and our traces show why that needs another look. Europe has started on lineage by requiring general-purpose model providers, open-source ones included, to publish a training-data summary, but a data summary won't show what a model's training sandboxes contained.

blocks.text: Governments have paid for this lesson before. After building Huawei and ZTE gear into their networks, Britain, Canada, and Germany set deadlines to tear it out, and the U.S. Congress had to find another $3.08 billion to help small carriers do the same. American police departments adopted Chinese robot dogs, and researchers found a hidden tunnel into one model's cameras and the same maker's humanoid robot streaming audio and video to servers in China. This July, the FCC banned new imports of foreign-made robot dogs and humanoids under the same 2019 law Congress wrote for Huawei. Hardware, at least, can be found and pulled out. Code a model wrote, scattered across thousands of repositories, is much harder to trace.

blocks.text: Why we test, and what trust requires

inlines.text: Why we test, and what trust requires

blocks.text: We found this because we test models the way our customers deploy them: as agents with real tools, inside sandboxes built to catch what they try to do. That includes models we don't make. We’re publishing what we found, including the hosts and the trigger, because the people deciding which models to trust need as much information as possible, and because security teams can act on it right away by blocking those hosts and watching for the trigger in their own systems.

blocks.text: Cohere is a global sovereign AI company serving enterprises across regulated industries, critical infrastructure, and sensitive government customers. Our view has always been that no organization should have to trust a black box blindly, whether it arrives as a weight file from a public hub or as an endpoint we can't see into. We build our own models, and the weights a customer runs in production come straight from us, with a single chain of custody. We track the lineage of our training data to guard against poisoning and malicious content. We can deploy where the customer's data already lives: in its own virtual private cloud, on its own servers, in a sovereign cloud, or fully air-gapped, with no Cohere access to that environment. And we open the hood for the security teams who have to sign off, walking them through where our training data came from, how our post-training and reinforcement-learning environments are built and cleaned, and what our red-teaming found.

blocks.text: What security teams and governments should do now

inlines.text: What security teams and governments should do now

blocks.text: For security teams:

inlines.text: For security teams:
Treat weights you didn't build like an unsigned binary, and enforce on the actual tool call before it runs. A reasoning trace is not a security boundary.
Deny agent egress by default.
Alert on cloud URLs you don't normally use or otherwise unexpected tool calls that aren’t mentioned in your day to day.
Block unprivileged user namespaces in agent containers, keep evaluation sandboxes away from production, and test AI-written code with live exploits.

blocks.text: Organizations buying AI systems should seek appropriate assurances regarding model provenance, training-environment security, and adversarial testing. Providers should be able to demonstrate that relevant risks have been assessed and mitigated through proportionate documentation, independent evaluations, or other trusted assurance mechanisms, while protecting proprietary and security-sensitive information.

blocks.text: Governments in Ottawa, Berlin, Washington, London, Brussels, Canberra, and Tokyo should require provenance and training-hygiene disclosures for critical and infrastructure uses, building on efforts like SP 800-218A. Restrictions on adversary-controlled models should state whether they cover the same weights running on government hardware. Allied AI safety institutes should run rare-event agentic testing like ours on popular open-weight models. And every allied market needs competitive, efficient models from builders willing to show their work.

blocks.text: Who is it calling?

inlines.text: Who is it calling?

blocks.text: Open-weight models will keep getting better and cheaper, and the pull to run them on your own hardware will only grow. Self-hosting decides where a model runs. Everything it learned in training, including the plumbing of the place it was trained, comes along. Know where your models came from, and work with builders who will show you. Then nobody has to wonder who their model is calling when no one is looking.
